samples.summary: Both write/draft endpoints are registered directly inside `configureServer`, so they sit AHEAD of Vite's internal host-check middleware and the origin guard is bypassable by DNS rebinding
samples.evidence:
`configureServer(server) { server.middlewares.use("/__wb_debug_report", …) }` (report-endpoint.ts:222-223, and again at :277) adds middleware synchronously in the hook. Vite only installs plugin middleware *after* its own internal middlewares when the hook RETURNS a function; middleware added directly is installed BEFORE them. Vite's `allowedHosts`/`hostCheckMiddleware` — the mitigation added for the dev-server DNS-rebinding CVE class — is one of those internal middlewares, so neither of these two endpoints is covered by it.

The only guard left is `isTrustedRequest` (line 124-144), which compares `Origin`'s host against the `Host` header and nothing else. Attack: attacker serves `http://evil.example:5173/` with a short TTL, then rebinds `evil.example` to 127.0.0.1. The victim's browser now treats `http://evil.example:5173/__wb_debug_report` as SAME-ORIGIN with the attacker's page — no preflight, no CORS involvement — and sends `Origin: http://evil.example:5173`, `Host: evil.example:5173`. Line 140 compares them, they are equal, so the request is trusted. `Content-Type: application/json` is freely settable on a same-origin fetch, so line 128 is no obstacle either.

What the attacker then gets, from an ordinary web page: (1) `writeFileSync` of attacker-chosen bytes into `<repoRoot>/.wb-reports/<attacker-chosen-sessionId>/*.png|jpg|webp` and `bundle.json` (lines 257-265) — arbitrary content in the developer's checkout, with the bundle text later consumed by the commit-capable intake pipeline; (2) unlimited use of the developer's Anthropic credential via `/__wb_debug_draft` with a fully attacker-authored prompt, and the completion is readable in the response (line 300). `isTrustedRequest` never checks that `Host` is a loopback name, which is the check the origin comparison silently assumes. Fix: return a post-hook from `configureServer` so the endpoints sit behind Vite's host check, and/or require `Host` to resolve to localhost/127.0.0.1/[::1].

samples.summary: `/__wb_debug_draft` spends the developer's model credential on a completely unvalidated, unbounded request body — no `parseBundle`, no item cap, no size cap, no rate limit
samples.evidence: The write endpoint runs the fail-closed `parseBundle` at line 236, but the draft endpoint only checks `typeof bundle === 'object'` (line 286) and hands the raw body straight to `draft(bundle as Parameters<typeof draftBundle>[0], …)` at line 290. `renderPrompt` (draft-endpoint.ts:112-130) then maps over `bundle.items` with no length limit, and `renderItem` interpolates `note`, `selector`, `text`, `address`, `tag`, `surface` verbatim. Combined with `MAX_BODY_BYTES = 64 * 1024 * 1024` (line 73), a single request can carry tens of thousands of items and drive an arbitrarily large input-token bill against `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`/the `ant auth login` profile resolved in `defaultClient()` (draft-endpoint.ts:170-173). Any script running on the app origin — an XSS, a dev fixture served from the project root, or the rebound-DNS page in the finding above — becomes a free, uncapped proxy to the credential, and reads the model's answer back at line 300. The design's security argument ("the worst case is a wasted token budget") is exactly this, but nothing bounds the budget.

samples.summary: `.wb-reports/` is not gitignored, so screenshots and bundle JSON written by the new endpoint land untracked in the checkout and can be committed and pushed
samples.evidence: `report-endpoint.ts:257-265` writes `<repoRoot>/.wb-reports/<sessionId>/{*.png|jpg|webp, bundle.json}` — captures of whatever was on the developer's screen (the design doc itself notes "a capture can contain another person's document"), plus the full bundle including `userAgent`, route and the reporter's text. Nothing in `.gitignore` matches: I read the whole file (195 lines) and grepped it for `wb-reports` and `.wb-` with no match. The analogous generated-artifact directories ARE ignored (`.harness-reports/` at line 173, `.hunt/` at line 194), so the omission is inconsistent as well as risky. A `git add -A` after a reporting session commits screenshots that may contain another user's document, a visible token, or an open `.env` in a nearby editor pane, and pushes them to a remote where they cannot be recalled.
searchedFor: grep -r 'wb-reports' across the repo (15 files; all source/docs/tests, no ignore rule)

samples.summary: Document/DOM text harvested from the page is interpolated into the drafting prompt, and the model's output is persisted into `.wb-reports/` for a commit-capable pipeline — an indirect prompt-injection path
samples.evidence: `renderItem` embeds `target.text`, `el.text`, `target.selector`, `target.address` and `item.note` into the user message (draft-endpoint.ts:86-109). For a `viewport` target these come from `elements[].text` — text scraped out of the rendered page, which in this app includes collaboratively-edited document content (Yorkie-backed docs/sheets, shared documents). A co-editor on a shared document can therefore plant instruction-shaped text that a developer unknowingly includes when reporting on that region. The model output is not merely displayed: `handOver` writes it into `item.draft` and the bundle is persisted to `.wb-reports/<session>/bundle.json` (report-endpoint.ts:262), which `scripts/agent/report-*.mjs` (PR 3, not yet present) reads with repository/commit credentials. The tool-free drafting call is the right mitigation for the drafting session itself, but nothing marks the injected text as untrusted for the downstream privileged reader, and `JSON.stringify` on the text only escapes quotes, not instructions. I could not complete the chain to a concrete commit because the intake runner does not exist on this branch — hence low confidence.

samples.summary: `sessionId` is fully caller-chosen, so any same-origin script can overwrite an already-approved `bundle.json` before the intake runner reads it
samples.evidence: `isSafeSegment(bundle.sessionId)` (line 244) only constrains the character set; it does not require the id to be one this server issued, nor does the write refuse an existing directory (`mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true })` at line 258, then unconditional `writeFileSync` at lines 260 and 262). A script on the app origin can enumerate/guess a queued session id — or simply reuse one it observed in the 200 response's `ref` field (line 270) — and replace both `bundle.json` and the images with different content. The developer's consent gate in the panel is then meaningless for that report: what intake reads is not what was approved. Writing with `flag: 'wx'`, or scoping the directory name to a server-generated id, closes this.

samples.summary: Up to 64 MB is buffered in memory per request before the size guard fires, and neither capture count nor total disk footprint is bounded
samples.evidence: `readJsonBody` pushes every chunk into `chunks` and only rejects once `size > MAX_BODY_BYTES` (lines 81-92) — by which point ~64 MB is resident. There is no concurrency limit, so a handful of parallel POSTs from a same-origin script exhaust the dev server's heap. Separately, `prepareCaptures` (lines 177-205) caps neither the number of captures nor their combined decoded size, and each accepted one becomes a `writeFileSync` (line 260), so a single accepted request can fill disk under `.wb-reports/`. Streaming the parse, or capping item/capture counts, would bound both.

samples.summary: A missing `Origin` header is treated as trusted, which is the one branch of the CSRF guard with no positive evidence behind it
samples.evidence: `if (origin === undefined) return { ok: true }; // same-origin fetch, or curl` (line 132). The comment's premise — that browsers always send `Origin` on POST — is true for current engines, so this is defensible today, but it is a fail-open default on an endpoint that writes into the repository and spends a credential: any client that omits the header (a stripping intermediary, an embedded webview, a future/legacy engine, a non-browser agent reached by SSRF from another local service) is granted the same authority as a same-origin page. A `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` requirement, or an explicit shared token minted by the plugin and injected into the page, would make the trusted case affirmative rather than inferred.

samples.summary: Arbitrary SDK/transport error messages are forwarded verbatim to the browser as `detail`
samples.evidence: Only `Anthropic.AuthenticationError` gets a sanitised message (lines 237-244); every other failure returns `detail: err.message` (line 249), which the plugin relays to the client at report-endpoint.ts:297 and the panel renders (`Drafting did not answer (${state.reason}: ${state.detail})`, panel.tsx). SDK/undici errors can carry proxy URLs, internal hostnames and request metadata from the dev-server environment into the page. A generic message plus a server-side log entry would keep the diagnostic without the disclosure.

verdict.reason: The described code exists exactly as claimed. Both `/__wb_debug_report` (report-endpoint.ts:223) and `/__wb_debug_draft` (report-endpoint.ts:277) are registered with `server.middlewares.use()` synchronously inside `configureServer` (line 222), and the hook returns no post-hook function (body closes at line 306). Per Vite's documented ordering, such middleware is installed BEFORE internal middlewares, so Vite 6.4's internal host-check/`allowedHosts` middleware (the DNS-rebinding mitigation; vite ^6.4.2 in packages/debug-report/package.json:33 and packages/frontend/package.json:107) never runs for these paths — the plugin handler responds first. The sole remaining gate, `isTrustedRequest` (lines 124-144), only requires `Content-Type: application/json` (line 128) and `new URL(origin).host === req.headers.host` (lines 136-142), with no loopback/allow-list check on `Host`, and it even returns ok when `Origin` is absent (line 132). Under DNS rebinding the attacker page is same-origin with the dev server, so Origin and Host match and the request is trusted with no preflight. Past the gate an attacker gets arbitrary file writes into the developer checkout (mkdirSync/writeFileSync, lines 257-265) and unlimited use of the developer's model credential with the completion returned to the attacker (lines 290-300). No mitigating guard exists elsewhere: the plugin is installed in a live dev server at packages/frontend/vite.config.ts:200, no vite.config.ts in the repo sets `server.allowedHosts` or constrains `server.host`, and packages/debug-report/src/plugin/index.ts:16-17 exports the plugin for other consumers as well. This is squarely in the security lane (bypassable CSRF/authorization gate plus credential exposure) and the file's own docstring at lines 23-27 relies on the very assumption that rebinding invalidates.

verdict.reason: Every claimed fact checks out verbatim. report-endpoint.ts:236 runs the fail-closed parseBundle on the write path, but the draft handler at report-endpoint.ts:286 does only `typeof bundle !== "object" || bundle === null` and then passes the raw request body to the credentialed model call via an unchecked `as` cast at report-endpoint.ts:290. MAX_BODY_BYTES = 64 MB (report-endpoint.ts:73) is the sole size bound. renderPrompt (draft-endpoint.ts:126) maps every element of bundle.items with no slice/cap, and renderItem (draft-endpoint.ts:82-110) interpolates note/tag/testId/selector/text/surface/address verbatim; the only cap is the per-item `.slice(0, 8)` on target.elements at line 98. I grepped the whole package for MAX_ITEMS|rateLimit|items.length|throttle|cap: the only server-side bound on the draft path is the non-empty check at draft-endpoint.ts:184. No item cap, no rate limit. defaultClient() (draft-endpoint.ts:170-173) constructs `new Anthropic()` with no explicit key, so the request is billed against ANTHROPIC_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN / the login profile in the dev-server process. The plugin is live via packages/frontend/vite.config.ts:200. The only gate, isTrustedRequest (report-endpoint.ts:124-144), is an origin gate rather than a content/volume gate, and it returns ok unconditionally when the Origin header is absent (line 132) — so any same-origin script, XSS, local process, or rebound-DNS page can drive an arbitrarily large input-token bill and read the answer at line 300. Not refutable: the code is present as described, no guard elsewhere bounds it, and it is in-lane as confused-deputy credential abuse via wholly unvalidated input on a credentialed operation whose sibling endpoint demonstrates the intended fail-closed validation. The tool-free request (no `tools` key, draft-endpoint.ts:209-210) and dev-only `apply: "serve"` (line 221) mitigate prompt-injection escalation but do nothing about the unbounded spend the file's own security argument (draft-endpoint.ts:8-10) rests on.

verdict.reason: Verified independently: report-endpoint.ts:63 sets REPORT_DIR=".wb-reports" and :257-265 mkdir/writeFileSync screenshots (png/jpg/webp) plus bundle.json under path.join(repoRoot, ".wb-reports", sessionId); vite.config.ts:200 sets repoRoot to the checkout root, so the artifacts land inside the working tree. I searched every ignore mechanism, not just the root file: root .gitignore (195 lines, read in full — ignores the analogous .harness-reports/:173, .worktrees/:180, .superpowers/:189, .hunt/:194, but nothing matching .wb-reports, and no incidental glob match), all nested ignore files (packages/frontend/.gitignore, packages/sheets/.gitignore, packages/backend/.gitignore — no .wb-/reports rule, and package-level files cannot cover a root path), .git/info/exclude (comments only, no active patterns), and the staging-time gate .githooks/pre-commit (docs/ path guard + `exec pnpm verify:fast`, no untracked-artifact or .wb-reports check). The endpoint also writes no self-ignoring .gitignore into the directory. So the omission is real and unguarded: arbitrary screen captures (which the design/task docs concede may show another person's document, and could show a token or an open .env pane) plus a bundle containing userAgent/route/reporter text sit untracked in the checkout and are swept up by `git add -A`, an irrecoverable sensitive-data exposure once pushed. In-lane for security as sensitive data exposure; severity major since exploitation requires developer error rather than an attacker action.

verdict.reason: The interpolation the reviewer cites is real (draft-endpoint.ts:82-110 embeds target.text/el.text/selector/address/item.note), but the impact chain that would make it blocking is guarded and, at its privileged end, absent. (1) The drafting request carries NO `tools` key and is schema-constrained (draft-endpoint.ts:200-211), so injected instructions have no privileged action and no egress channel — the worst case is altered draft prose. (2) The draft is surfaced as editable title/body fields (panel.tsx:427-452) and nothing is persisted until the reporter explicitly clicks "Hand over" (panel.tsx:289-305); malformed drafts are refused wholesale (handover.ts:80-89). (3) The claimed credentialed sink does not exist in this repository: `Glob scripts/agent/report*` returns no files, and grepping `wb-reports`, `bundle.json`, and `debug-report` across `scripts/` finds no reader of `.wb-reports/` at all (only scripts/verify-self.mjs:343-345, which runs typecheck/tests). The reviewer concedes the intake runner is "PR 3, not yet present". (4) Both endpoints are dev-server-only (report-endpoint.ts:221, apply: "serve") behind an origin+content-type CSRF gate (report-endpoint.ts:124-144). Additionally, the raw harvested text lands in bundle.json independently of the drafting call, so untrusted-content marking is a concern owned by any future intake reader, not by this diff. What remains here is a hardening suggestion (delimit untrusted page text in the prompt), which is minor/nit under this lens's rubric, not a blocking authz/secret/injection/crypto break.
